events.title: Bacon's Rebellion Burns Jamestown
events.blurb: A Virginia planter named Nathaniel Bacon rallied a mixed force of frontier settlers, indentured servants, and enslaved Africans against the colonial governor and marched on the capital, burning Jamestown to the ground. The uprising — the largest armed revolt in colonial America before the Revolution — exposed deep class and racial tensions that led planters to harden the legal distinction between Black slaves and white laborers.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1676 — Jamestown, Virginia. Bacon died of dysentery six weeks after burning the capital, ending the rebellion without a battle. Historians argue his multiracial army scared Virginia's elite so badly they accelerated the shift to race-based chattel slavery.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Battle of New Orleans
events.blurb: General Andrew Jackson's patchwork army of Tennessee frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, free Black soldiers, Choctaw warriors, and pirates under Jean Lafitte decisively routed an 8,000-strong British force attempting to seize New Orleans, killing or wounding roughly 2,000 redcoats while suffering fewer than 70 American casualties. The lopsided victory made Jackson a national hero and propelled him to the presidency.
events.revealBlurb: January 8, 1815 — Chalmette, Louisiana. The Treaty of Ghent ending the War of 1812 had been signed 15 days earlier — news hadn't arrived. The battle had zero effect on the war's official outcome but enormous effect on American mythology and Jackson's political career.

events.title: Battle of Gettysburg Begins
events.blurb: Confederate soldiers advancing through a Pennsylvania town accidentally encountered Union cavalry, triggering three days of fighting that became the bloodiest battle ever fought on American soil. A total of approximately 50,000 soldiers were killed, wounded, or went missing — roughly one in three of all combatants engaged on both sides.

events.title: Spanish-American War Declaration
events.blurb: The United States declared war on Spain following the mysterious explosion of the battleship USS Maine in Havana Harbor and years of lurid coverage of Spanish atrocities in Cuba by the American yellow press. The 114-day conflict ended Spanish colonial rule in Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines, and announced the United States as a Pacific and Caribbean imperial power.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 1898 — Washington, D.C. Theodore Roosevelt resigned as Assistant Secretary of the Navy to lead the volunteer Rough Riders cavalry regiment, charging up San Juan Hill — a battle that took one afternoon and made him president. Secretary of State John Hay called it "a splendid little war."

events.title: Amelia Earhart Solos the Atlantic
events.blurb: A 34-year-old American aviator landed her red single-engine Lockheed Vega in a farmer's meadow in northern Ireland after a 15-hour, 3,260-kilometre flight from Newfoundland, becoming the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. The trip had included an altimeter failure, engine icing, and a broken exhaust manifold that spewed flames into the cockpit for the last eight hours.
events.revealBlurb: May 20-21, 1932 — exactly five years after Charles Lindbergh's crossing. Earhart had originally meant to land in Paris; she turned toward the nearest pasture when she smelled fuel. She had been the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air four years earlier, but only as a passenger.

events.title: Amelia Earhart Disappears
events.blurb: On the penultimate leg of an around-the-world flight at the equator, a 39-year-old American aviator and her navigator took off from a Pacific airstrip bound for a tiny coral island 4,100 kilometres away. Her final radio messages reported low fuel and inability to locate the island. A Navy search of 400,000 square kilometres of ocean found nothing. Her disappearance has launched a hundred books and at least three feature films.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1937 — Earhart and Fred Noonan bound for Howland Island. Prevailing theories: ran out of fuel and ditched; landed on uninhabited Nikumaroro and died of thirst; captured by the Japanese. No conclusive physical evidence exists.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Sandra Day O'Connor Confirmed
events.blurb: A 51-year-old former state senator and state appellate judge from the American Southwest was confirmed by the U.S. Senate 99-0 as the first woman to sit on the U.S. Supreme Court, fulfilling a campaign promise the president who had nominated her made during the 1980 election. She would serve 24 years, writing decisions on affirmative action, abortion, and the disputed 2000 election.
events.revealBlurb: September 21, 1981 — confirmed; Ronald Reagan had nominated her. Her 2005 retirement was precipitated by her husband's declining health from Alzheimer's. She herself was diagnosed with dementia in 2018 and died in 2023.

events.title: Geraldine Ferraro Nominated for VP
events.blurb: A three-term congresswoman from Queens, New York, was nominated as the vice-presidential candidate on a major U.S. political party's ticket — the first woman in either party's history to reach such a position. The Democratic ticket she joined lost 49 of 50 states to the Republican incumbent five months later, but a barrier had been broken.
events.revealBlurb: July 19, 1984 — accepted by acclamation at the Democratic National Convention in San Francisco. Running mate Walter Mondale lost in a Reagan landslide. It would be 24 years before another woman appeared on a major-party ticket (Sarah Palin, 2008).

events.title: Citizen Kane Released
events.blurb: A 25-year-old radio and theatre prodigy made his feature film directing debut with a quasi-biographical study of a newspaper tycoon, structurally organized as a series of flashback interviews about the man's last word ("Rosebud"). The film used deep-focus cinematography, low-angle setups, overlapping dialogue, and non-linear structure in ways that rewrote the cinematic grammar of the next 70 years. Its real-life subject, a media baron, tried to have every print destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1941 — Orson Welles, age 25. The target was William Randolph Hearst, who banned mention of the film in his newspapers. It lost Best Picture to "How Green Was My Valley." It tops nearly every "greatest films of all time" list.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Rashomon Released
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Japanese director released a 88-minute film in which the same violent encounter is recounted by four different participants, none of whom agrees with any of the others. The Venice Film Festival awarded it the Golden Lion the following year, and the world film industry discovered Japanese cinema as a major force. The very title became an English noun: "the Rashomon effect" is the concept of contradictory memories.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1950 — Akira Kurosawa. The producers were reportedly baffled by the script and wanted it re-edited. Its Venice win completely blindsided Japanese critics, who had not thought much of the film. It led directly to the global reception of Ozu, Mizoguchi, and Kurosawa's later work.

events.title: Fellini's 8½ Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a semi-autobiographical film about a filmmaker suffering a creative block while preparing his next picture, in which the director's own memories, dreams, and erotic fantasies dissolve into the plot he is trying to construct. The Italian title referred literally to the number of films the director had made. It won two Oscars and became the classic film-about-film-making, endlessly quoted by later directors similarly stuck.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 1963 — Federico Fellini, with Marcello Mastroianni as his alter ego. Fellini had genuinely been blocked after a string of successes; the film emerged from trying to work out why. It was remade as a Broadway musical ("Nine") in 1982.

events.title: Back to the Future Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old director released a 116-minute time-travel comedy about a teenager who accidentally travels 30 years into his own past and must ensure his parents fall in love so he himself will exist. The original cast had been halfway through shooting with a different lead actor when the director fired him and reshot the entire film with a new star. The resulting product became the top-grossing film of its year and spawned two sequels.
events.revealBlurb: July 3, 1985 — Robert Zemeckis, starring Michael J. Fox and Christopher Lloyd. The original Marty was Eric Stoltz; replacing him cost $4 million in reshoots. The DeLorean was Zemeckis's choice — he wanted a time machine that looked, plausibly, like a spaceship.

events.title: Virgil's Aeneid
events.blurb: A 51-year-old Roman poet died with his commissioned national epic not quite finished, asking on his deathbed that the unfinished manuscript be burned. The emperor he had spent a decade writing it for overruled him. The twelve-book poem traced the mythical origins of Rome to a Trojan prince fleeing the burning city. It became, and remains, the canonical literary masterpiece of Latin civilization.
events.revealBlurb: 19 BCE — Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro). Emperor Augustus saved the text. Virgil's funeral procession was attended by the emperor himself. Dante took Virgil as his guide through Hell and Purgatory in The Divine Comedy; Milton modeled Paradise Lost on the Aeneid.

events.title: Alice in Wonderland Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Oxford mathematics don who had developed a story three years earlier during a boating trip with three little girls, the daughter of the dean of his college, published a book-length expansion of it. The nonsense-logic adventures of a curious girl falling into a subterranean world of mad tea parties, playing-card royalty, and cat grins without cats became the foundation text of modern children's literature.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1865 — Charles Dodgson, pen name Lewis Carroll. Alice Liddell was the model; their rowboat trip on July 4, 1862 was three years earlier to the day. The 1862 handwritten original, illustrated by Carroll, was given to Alice; it is now in the British Library.

events.title: Treasure Island Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish writer, suffering severe pulmonary illness and convalescing in the Scottish Highlands, sketched a treasure map with his 12-year-old stepson on a rainy afternoon and began improvising a story for the boy. The serialized pirate adventure novel that grew from the map — featuring a peg-legged cook, a squawking parrot, a buried fortune, and a black spot — essentially defined the iconography of piracy for the next century and a half.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 1883 — Robert Louis Stevenson. Initially serialized in the magazine Young Folks in 1881 as "The Sea Cook." The phrase "Shiver me timbers!" does not appear in the book but was popularized by its Long John Silver.

events.title: First Nobel Prize in Literature
events.blurb: A Swedish Academy of cultural grandees, following the will of the dynamite inventor who had died five years earlier leaving his fortune to fund annual prizes, selected a 62-year-old French poet as the first recipient of their literature award. Their choice was safe, genteel, and now obscure; they had passed over Leo Tolstoy, widely considered Europe's greatest living novelist. The omission has dogged the Nobel Literature Prize's reputation ever since.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1901 — Sully Prudhomme. Other early laureates passed over: Tolstoy, Chekhov, Ibsen, Zola, Mark Twain. The prize included 150,782 Swedish kronor — a substantial sum in 1901, about $3.5 million today.

events.title: To Kill a Mockingbird Published
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Alabama-born New York airline reservation clerk published her first and, for over half a century, only novel — a semi-autobiographical story narrated by a six-year-old white girl whose father, a small-town Southern lawyer, defends a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. The book won a Pulitzer the next year and has been a school-curriculum fixture in the U.S. ever since.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 1960 — Harper Lee. Her childhood friend Truman Capote was the model for the character Dill. Gregory Peck won an Oscar for the film adaptation. Lee published a second novel, "Go Set a Watchman," in 2015, a year before her death; it was an earlier draft of the same book.

events.title: Bach Dedicates Brandenburg Concertos
events.blurb: A 36-year-old German court composer, looking for a new job, sent a margrave a set of six concerto grossi he had been accumulating over several years. The dedication was effusive; he apologized for the "vast distance between his person and the margrave." The margrave never acknowledged the gift, let alone hired him, and probably never had them performed. The manuscripts sat in a Prussian archive for 128 years before rediscovery.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1721 — Johann Sebastian Bach, addressing Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg. The scores were narrowly rescued from Allied bombing in 1945. The music now exists thanks to a librarian who grabbed them as he fled Leipzig for the Harz mountains.

events.title: Wagner's Ring Cycle Premieres
events.blurb: A 63-year-old German composer presented the first complete four-night performance of a 15-hour operatic cycle he had been writing, off and on, for 26 years, at a festival opera house in a Bavarian town he had specifically had built to host it. Audiences included Tchaikovsky, Liszt, Grieg, Bruckner, the emperor of Germany, and the emperor of Brazil. The complete run was a financial disaster.
events.revealBlurb: August 13-17, 1876 — Richard Wagner at the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, Bayreuth. The festival runs to this day; tickets are difficult to obtain. Wagner's anti-Semitic essays, and the Nazi regime's later embrace of his work, have cast a lasting shadow.

events.title: Elvis Records "That's All Right"
events.blurb: During a break in a fruitless recording session in Memphis, a 19-year-old truck driver began playing an uptempo blues song with such energy that the studio owner halted the session, rewound the tape, and asked him to do it again from the start. The recording blended country and rhythm-and-blues in a style that had no existing commercial category.

events.title: Elvis's First Sun Session
events.blurb: A 19-year-old truck driver who had walked into a small Memphis recording studio a year earlier to make an acetate for his mother's birthday showed up for a late-night try-out with two local session musicians. The session was going nowhere until, during a break, the kid started goofing around with an old R&B song by Arthur Crudup. The engineer slapped the tape on and caught it. Within weeks the song was a regional hit.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1954 — Elvis Presley, Scotty Moore, and Bill Black at Sun Records, Memphis. The song was "That's All Right (Mama)." Studio owner Sam Phillips had famously said he could make "a billion dollars" if he could find a white man who sang with a Black feel.

events.title: Woodstock Festival
events.blurb: A three-day music festival, overcapacity within hours of opening, drew an estimated 400,000 young people to a dairy farm in upstate New York despite severe rain. Fences collapsed; the event became de facto free. 32 acts performed — Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, The Who, Santana, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Joan Baez. Two people died (one from an overdose, one crushed by a tractor); two babies were born. The festival became the defining symbol of the 1960s counterculture.
events.revealBlurb: August 15-18, 1969 — on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, NY. Hendrix closed at 9 AM Monday morning to a dwindling crowd with a distorted, feedback-laced "Star-Spangled Banner." The 1970 documentary won an Oscar.

events.title: Semmelweis and Handwashing
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Hungarian-born obstetrician in a Vienna maternity hospital observed that the ward staffed by medical students (who also performed autopsies) had a puerperal-fever death rate three times higher than the ward staffed by midwives. He instituted compulsory chlorinated-lime handwashing and watched the death rate drop tenfold. The medical establishment rejected his findings; he was dismissed, ridiculed, and eventually committed to an asylum, where he died of injuries from a beating by guards.
events.revealBlurb: 1847 — Ignaz Semmelweis at Vienna General Hospital. His theory was resisted because germ theory didn't yet exist; doctors took offense at being blamed for patient deaths. He died in an asylum on August 13, 1865, ironically of an infection from his beating injuries. Germ theory vindicated him a few years later.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine Used on a Human
events.blurb: A French chemist administered the first human dose of an experimental rabies treatment to a nine-year-old boy who had been severely bitten by a rabid dog two days earlier and faced certain death without intervention. The boy survived, and the successful case launched the practice of post-exposure vaccination for infectious disease.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine
events.blurb: A 62-year-old French chemist, who had been working for years on vaccines against animal diseases, administered his experimental rabies vaccine — desiccated spinal cord tissue from infected rabbits — to a 9-year-old Alsatian boy who had been savaged by a rabid dog two days earlier. The boy received 13 injections over ten days and survived. Rabies, previously universally fatal once symptoms appeared, now had an effective post-exposure prophylaxis.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 1885 — Louis Pasteur; patient was Joseph Meister. Pasteur was not licensed as a physician; he could have been prosecuted if the boy had died. Meister grew up, became the gatekeeper at the Institut Pasteur, and is said to have killed himself in 1940 rather than let Nazi troops enter Pasteur's tomb (disputed; he may have died from gas poisoning unrelated).

events.title: Röntgen Discovers X-Rays
events.blurb: A 50-year-old German physicist, working with a cathode-ray tube covered in black cardboard, noticed that a paper screen coated in barium platinocyanide glowed even when placed some distance away. He realized the tube was emitting an invisible, unknown type of radiation. Further experiments showed the rays penetrated paper, wood, aluminum, and even human flesh — but not bone. He published an image of his wife's hand, showing her skeleton and wedding ring.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1895 — Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen at the University of Würzburg. He called the phenomenon "X" rays because he didn't know what they were. He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. The image of his wife's hand, published in early 1896, is arguably the first diagnostic X-ray.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: Newton's Principia Published
events.blurb: A three-volume work laid out universal laws of motion and gravitation in mathematical form, explaining why apples fall and why planets orbit in ellipses with a single unified framework. The laws held that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1687 — Edmond Halley paid for the printing out of his own pocket after the Royal Society spent its book budget on a history of fishes. Newton later said a dispute over priority with Robert Hooke was the reason he almost withheld the whole thing.

events.title: Animal Electricity Discovered
events.blurb: An Italian physician published a decade of experiments showing that the muscles of dead frogs could be made to contract when touched with two different metals — or when connected to a charged conductor — demonstrating that animal tissues themselves generate and respond to electrical currents. The finding launched the science of electrophysiology and inspired fierce debate about the nature of electricity and life.
events.revealBlurb: 1791 — Luigi Galvani called the phenomenon "animal electricity"; Alessandro Volta argued it was purely metallic electricity and invented the first battery to prove the point. Both were partly right. The argument inspired Mary Shelley: she attended a lecture on Galvanic reanimation and later wrote Frankenstein.

events.title: Uncertainty Principle Formulated
events.blurb: A paper established that it is fundamentally impossible to know both the exact position and exact momentum of a quantum particle simultaneously — the more precisely one is measured, the less precisely the other can be known, not because of measurement limitations but as a feature of nature itself. The principle implied that determinism at the subatomic scale was not merely unknown but unknowable.
events.revealBlurb: March 1927 — Werner Heisenberg derived the uncertainty principle while working alone in Copenhagen, having sent Niels Bohr on vacation. Bohr returned and disputed the physical interpretation, sparking weeks of argument. Albert Einstein spent years devising thought experiments to disprove the principle; Bohr refuted each one.

events.title: Cosmic Microwave Background Detected
events.blurb: Two radio astronomers testing a sensitive antenna at a New Jersey laboratory detected an inexplicable low-level microwave hiss coming equally from every direction in the sky, regardless of season or time of day. Unable to explain it as noise — including suspected pigeon droppings on the antenna — they eventually learned that theorists nearby had predicted exactly such radiation as the afterglow of the universe's earliest moments.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1964 — Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson initially assumed the noise was instrument error or interference from New York City. They famously removed a pair of pigeons that had nested in the antenna and cleaned out the "white dielectric material." The theorists at Princeton, who had been preparing to search for the signal, were beaten to the discovery.

events.title: Higgs Boson Announced
events.blurb: At a packed seminar, two independent experimental teams working at the world's largest particle accelerator announced the observation of a new particle consistent with the long-predicted Higgs boson — the quantum field excitation that gives other fundamental particles their mass. The discovery completed the standard model of particle physics, confirming a prediction made nearly fifty years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 2012 — Peter Higgs, who had predicted the boson in 1964, was in the audience and reportedly wept. The two experiments — ATLAS and CMS — had been run in blind competition to avoid bias. Higgs and François Englert shared the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year.

events.title: New Coke Launched
events.blurb: A 99-year-old American beverage company launched a reformulated version of its flagship cola, sweeter and smoother, aimed at winning back market share from Pepsi in a rivalry called the Cola Wars. Blind taste tests had shown a preference for the new recipe; actual consumer response, once they knew what they were drinking, was widespread rage. Letters of protest poured into Atlanta; soda fountains advertised the return of the original. 79 days later, the company announced the comeback of "Coca-Cola Classic."
events.revealBlurb: April 23, 1985 — Coca-Cola. The original formula returned as "Coca-Cola Classic" on July 11, 1985. New Coke eventually became "Coke II" in 1992 and was quietly discontinued in 2002. The whole episode is now a business-school case study in consumer-brand attachment.

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: O.J. Simpson Bronco Chase
events.blurb: A 46-year-old former football star, charged with the murders of his ex-wife and her friend, failed to surrender to police at the agreed time. A friend drove him along a Los Angeles freeway in a white Ford Bronco at around 55 km/h, pursued by police cruisers and a dozen news helicopters. An estimated 95 million Americans watched the chase live on television. It ended with his surrender at his home.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1994 — O.J. Simpson, driver Al Cowlings. NBC interrupted Game 5 of the NBA Finals between the Knicks and Rockets to show the chase. Simpson was acquitted of murder on October 3, 1995 in what was nicknamed the "Trial of the Century."

events.title: Spice Girls' "Wannabe"
events.blurb: A British pop group of five young women released their debut single — a bouncy three-minute track with a rap-like opening, shot on a single take in a Lisbon hotel — hit number one in 37 countries over the following months. The five — styled "Scary," "Sporty," "Baby," "Ginger," and "Posh" — would dominate late-1990s pop culture with a "Girl Power" message that was earnest, commercial, and enormously successful. They sold 100 million records globally.
events.revealBlurb: July 8, 1996 — Spice Girls: Melanie B (Scary), Melanie C (Sporty), Emma Bunton (Baby), Geri Halliwell (Ginger), Victoria Adams (Posh). The video was shot in a single day at the Hotel Palácio in Portugal. Victoria Beckham married David Beckham in 1999; she launched a fashion career later.

events.title: Princess Diana Dies
events.blurb: A 36-year-old former British princess and two others died in a high-speed car crash in an underpass in central Paris after their driver attempted to evade pursuing paparazzi. Her death — ten months after her divorce from the heir to the British throne — triggered a massive public outpouring of grief that caught the British monarchy off guard. Over a million bouquets of flowers were left at London's royal palaces. Her funeral a week later was watched by 2.5 billion people globally.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1997 — Diana, Princess of Wales at the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. Her companion Dodi Fayed and the drunk driver Henri Paul also died; bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived. Elton John performed a rewritten "Candle in the Wind" at the funeral, which became the best-selling single of all time.

events.title: Lascaux Cave Paintings
events.blurb: In a limestone complex in southwestern France, Paleolithic artists over multiple generations painted some 6,000 bulls, deer, horses, and abstract signs along narrow corridors and a soaring "Hall of the Bulls" as large as a Romanesque nave. The largest painted bull is over five metres long. The cave was rediscovered in 1940 by four teenagers and their dog investigating a tree that had been uprooted by a storm.
events.revealBlurb: c. 17,000 BCE — Montignac, Dordogne. The original cave was closed to visitors in 1963 when tourist breath and carbon dioxide began damaging the pigments. Lascaux II, III, and IV — increasingly faithful replicas — have been opened to the public.

events.title: Rembrandt's Night Watch
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Dutch painter completed a 3.6 by 4.4 metre group portrait of an Amsterdam militia company, commissioned by 18 civic-guard officers each paying 100 guilders for his place. Unlike the static lineup portraits typical of the genre, the painter depicted the company in motion, emerging from a shadowed arch with a drum rolling and a musket firing. The title "Night Watch" is a misnomer added by 19th-century curators; varnish had darkened a daytime scene.
events.revealBlurb: 1642 — Rembrandt van Rijn. Now in Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum. It was trimmed on all sides in 1715 to fit between two doorways, losing two figures. A recent 8K restoration reconstructed the missing pieces using AI.

events.title: Velázquez's Las Meninas
events.blurb: A court painter completed a 3.2-metre oil depicting a 5-year-old Spanish princess surrounded by her ladies-in-waiting, two dwarfs, a dog, and — impossibly — himself at his easel. A distant mirror on the back wall reflects the figures of her parents, the king and queen, who appear to be standing exactly where the viewer stands. The painting is essentially a visual puzzle about who is depicting whom and from where.
events.revealBlurb: 1656 — Diego Velázquez at the Spanish court. The princess is Margarita Teresa. Now in Madrid's Prado. Picasso painted 58 variations on it in 1957. Foucault opened his book The Order of Things with a long reading of its perspective.

events.title: Hokusai's Great Wave
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Japanese printmaker produced the first of thirty-six woodblock prints depicting views of a sacred mountain, all showing it from different perspectives and in different weather. The first print, which viewers sometimes mistook for the title piece, showed an enormous wave curling in threatening foam over three small fishing boats, with the mountain a distant cone between its spray. The distinctive blue pigment, Prussian blue, was a recent European import.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1831 — Katsushika Hokusai. The print is one of the most widely reproduced images in the world; thousands of impressions survive. Hokusai called himself "the old man mad about drawing" and claimed he would become a true artist only at 110.

events.title: First Impressionist Exhibition
events.blurb: Thirty painters whose work had been repeatedly rejected by the official French Salon rented the studio of a photographer on a Paris boulevard and held their own group show. A review in a satirical magazine mocked one of the paintings — "Impression, Sunrise" — and gave the movement the name it would keep. The show attracted 3,500 visitors, which was dismal; mockery outweighed admiration; most of the painters struggled financially for another decade.
events.revealBlurb: April 15 to May 15, 1874 — 35 Boulevard des Capucines, Paris. Participants included Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro, Cézanne, Berthe Morisot, and Sisley. The critic who coined the term, Louis Leroy, titled his review "Exhibition of the Impressionists" sarcastically; the painters adopted it.

events.title: Battle of Britain
events.blurb: For nearly four months, an island nation's outnumbered fighter force faced daily mass raids by the world's most battle-hardened air force, with the explicit goal of destroying aerial defences so that a seaborne invasion could follow. Radar stations, sector control rooms, and the pilots' ability to keep flying became the three fulcrums on which the outcome balanced.
events.revealBlurb: July 10 – October 31, 1940. The RAF lost 1,023 aircraft; the Luftwaffe lost 1,887. Churchill's "The Few" speech on August 20 honoured the pilots — the average age of whom was just 20. Germany quietly postponed its invasion plan on September 17 and never rescheduled it.

events.title: Lend-Lease Act Signed
events.blurb: A nation officially at peace passed legislation allowing its president to lend, lease, or otherwise transfer war materials to any country whose defence he deemed vital to national security, bypassing a strict neutrality law without technically entering the conflict. The first shipments moved within weeks, directed at an island nation running critically short of everything.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 1941 — FDR signed H.R. 1776 (the bill number was a deliberate wink). By the end of the programme, the US had shipped $50 billion in supplies — equivalent to roughly $800 billion today — to 38 countries. The Soviet Union received about 17 million tons of equipment, including 400,000 jeeps and trucks.

events.title: Dieppe Raid
events.blurb: Roughly 6,000 troops — mostly Canadians — landed in daylight on a heavily defended beach overlooked by cliffs and were cut down before many could clear the waterline, suffering nearly 60 percent casualties in under ten hours. Planners later claimed the catastrophic failure provided lessons that saved countless lives in subsequent amphibious operations.
events.revealBlurb: August 19, 1942 — Operation Jubilee. Of 4,963 Canadians who embarked, only 2,210 returned to England; 907 were killed and 1,946 taken prisoner. The Germans, who had received advance intelligence, held their positions with minimal effort. Churchill admitted privately it was "a very heavy and grievous loss."

events.title: Battle of Kursk
events.blurb: Two million soldiers and nearly 6,000 tanks clashed around a salient in the steppe, with the attackers driving into prepared defences twelve layers deep that had been built specifically to absorb and exhaust an armoured offensive. For the first time in the eastern conflict, a major German armoured attack was stopped before achieving a breakthrough.
events.revealBlurb: July 5 – August 23, 1943. The Germans had repeatedly delayed the offensive to wait for newer tanks, giving Soviet intelligence — fed by the British Ultra intercepts — five months to prepare. The opening day, July 5, was the single costliest day in the history of aerial warfare by aircraft lost. Germany never regained strategic initiative in the East afterward.

events.title: Rosie the Riveter Campaign
events.blurb: A deliberate government and industry campaign to recruit women into heavy industrial and weapons manufacturing work portrayed a bandana-wearing figure flexing her arm above the slogan "We Can Do It!" alongside magazine illustrations that reached millions of households, reshaping public expectations of gender and labour across a nation at industrial-scale mobilisation.
events.revealBlurb: 1942–1943. The number of women in the US workforce rose from 12 million to 20 million — a 57% increase — by 1944. Women built B-29s, welded Liberty ships, and operated cranes. The Westinghouse "We Can Do It!" poster was seen by almost no one during the war; it was rediscovered in the 1980s and became an icon of the feminist movement.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Avignon Papacy Begins
events.blurb: A French-born pope, under pressure from the French king and unable to safely reside in Rome because of factional warfare among Italian noble families, transferred the papal court across the Alps to a southern French town on the Rhône. For the next 68 years, seven successive popes — all French — would rule the Western church from there, deeply compromising papal prestige.
events.revealBlurb: 1309 — Pope Clement V. Critics called it the "Babylonian Captivity of the Church." The papacy returned to Rome in 1377, only to split almost immediately into rival popes in Rome and Avignon.

events.title: Joan of Arc Burned at the Stake
events.blurb: A 19-year-old French woman, captured by Burgundian allies of the English and sold to the English crown for 10,000 livres, was tried for heresy by a church court and burned to death in a market square of a Norman city. Her executioners dug through the embers to prove she had died rather than escaped. Her remains were thrown into the Seine. She was canonized by the Vatican 489 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 1431 — Rouen. A retrial in 1456 cleared her of all charges. The principal heresy she had refused to recant was wearing men's clothes. She became a Catholic saint in 1920 — six years after French troops carried her image into the trenches of World War I.

events.title: Fall of Granada
events.blurb: The last Muslim ruler of an Andalusian emirate, besieged for seven months in his Alhambra palace, handed over its keys to Castilian and Aragonese monarchs and rode into exile, reportedly sighing at his final view from a mountain pass. The surrender ended 781 years of Muslim political presence on the Iberian peninsula. The same monarchs, three months later, would commission an Italian sailor to seek a western route to Asia.
events.revealBlurb: January 2, 1492 — Ferdinand and Isabella accept the surrender of Muhammad XII (Boabdil). His mother is said to have told him: "You weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man." Columbus was at the Alhambra that summer presenting his proposal.

events.title: Bayeux Tapestry Completed
events.blurb: An embroidered strip of linen 70 metres long and 50 centimetres high, worked in coloured wool yarns, depicts in 58 scenes the Norman conquest of a cross-Channel kingdom — the diplomatic prelude, the invasion fleet, a victorious battle, and the death of a king by arrow. It includes 623 human figures, 202 horses, 55 dogs, and a Latin commentary running across the top.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1077 — commissioned either by Bishop Odo of Bayeux or Queen Matilda. Despite its name, it is technically embroidery, not tapestry. It survived the French Revolution only because a local lawyer hid it when a crowd tried to use it to cover an ammunition wagon.

events.title: Caravaggio's Calling of St Matthew
events.blurb: A 28-year-old painter completed the first of three monumental canvases for a chapel in a Roman church, depicting the moment when Christ walks into a tax collector's office and wordlessly summons a clerk to follow him. A shaft of natural light cuts diagonally across the scene, picking out faces from deep shadow. The painter used Roman street-people as models and dressed the apostles in contemporary clothes. The effect shocked and recruited a generation of imitators across Europe.
events.revealBlurb: 1600 — Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio, at the Contarelli Chapel, San Luigi dei Francesi. Art historians still argue about which figure is Matthew. The painter killed a man in a brawl six years later and died on the run at 38.

events.title: Munch's The Scream
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Norwegian painter completed the first version of a composition he had been sketching for years, showing a androgynous figure with an egg-shaped face and open mouth on a bridge above a blood-orange sky. The painter later wrote of the walk at dusk during which he had felt "a shriek passing through nature." He produced four versions across several decades; two have been stolen, and both were recovered.
events.revealBlurb: 1893 — Edvard Munch. The sky's colour may be real: it has been linked to the atmospheric effects of the Krakatoa eruption ten years earlier. The Oslo theft in 1994 happened during the opening ceremony of the Winter Olympics. The thieves left a note: "Thanks for the poor security."

events.title: Picasso's Guernica
events.blurb: A Spanish painter in his mid-fifties produced a 3.5-metre-tall monochrome canvas for the Spanish pavilion at a Paris international exposition, depicting the destruction of a Basque town by Nazi and Fascist bombers at the request of the Spanish Nationalist forces a month earlier. Screaming women, a dismembered soldier, a wounded horse, a bull, and a single lightbulb-like eye crowd the picture. The artist refused to have it displayed in his homeland until fascist rule there ended.
events.revealBlurb: Painted January-June 1937; exhibited July 12 at the Paris Exhibition. Picasso. The bombing of Guernica was on April 26, 1937. The painting toured the world for 40 years, then was installed in Madrid in 1981, six years after Franco's death.

events.title: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans
events.blurb: A 33-year-old former commercial illustrator exhibited 32 canvases, each showing a single can of condensed soup — one for each of the 32 varieties the food company then sold. He had painted them by projecting photographic images onto the canvas and tracing. The show sold modestly: five of the canvases went for $100 each; the gallery owner bought them back and later resold the whole set for $2 million.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1962 — Ferus Gallery, Los Angeles, Andy Warhol. The artist said he ate Campbell's soup every day for 20 years. The set is now in MoMA. Warhol would soon apply the same silk-screen methods to Marilyn Monroe, Jackie Kennedy, and Elvis.

events.title: Louis Armstrong's Hot Fives
events.blurb: A 24-year-old cornetist who had grown up in the poorest section of New Orleans walked into a Chicago studio for the first session with a small band of his own. Over the next three years, the "Hot Five" and "Hot Seven" sessions would reshape popular music. His vocal improvisation on "Heebie Jeebies" — a chorus of nonsense syllables when he claimed to drop his lyric sheet — launched scat singing. His trumpet solos made the individual improvisation the heart of jazz.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1925 — Louis Armstrong at OKeh Records, Chicago. The "Heebie Jeebies" vocal made him a national figure. He would become the first African-American to host a nationally sponsored radio show.

events.title: Beatles on Ed Sullivan
events.blurb: Four young British musicians from a northwestern English port city performed live on a Sunday-evening American variety show before an audience of 73 million viewers — at the time the largest in U.S. television history. The hysteria had preceded them: 7,000 people had mobbed their arrival at a New York airport two days earlier. Adult commentators dismissed them as a passing fad; younger Americans rearranged their evening to watch.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1964 — The Beatles at Studio 50, Manhattan. The crime rate during the broadcast was unusually low — even, it was said, in Times Square. They returned the next two Sundays for back-to-back appearances.

events.title: Monterey Pop Festival
events.blurb: A three-day rock festival on a California coastal fairground — the first major rock festival of the decade and the template for what came later — introduced American audiences to a left-handed guitarist recently returned from London, a young Otis Redding, and Janis Joplin. The left-hander, during his set, laid his guitar on the stage, knelt over it, and set it on fire with lighter fluid. The audience had not imagined such a thing was possible.
events.revealBlurb: June 16-18, 1967 — the guitarist was Jimi Hendrix, on the closing Sunday. Monterey Pop Festival drew 200,000 people. The Mamas & the Papas had organized it; proceeds went to charity. Paul McCartney recommended Hendrix and The Who to the organizers.

events.title: Live Aid
events.blurb: Two simultaneous 16-hour benefit concerts, one at a stadium in London and one at a stadium in Philadelphia, were broadcast live to an estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 countries — at the time perhaps 40 percent of the world population. The concerts raised around $127 million for Ethiopian famine relief. A British band's 21-minute set, by most accounts, stole the whole day. Its lead singer's synchronized clap-along with 72,000 people is the stuff of legend.
events.revealBlurb: July 13, 1985 — Wembley Stadium and JFK Stadium. The stealing-the-show band was Queen, Freddie Mercury at Wembley. Co-organizers Bob Geldof and Midge Ure. "Feed the World" had been launched by the Band Aid charity single the previous Christmas.

events.title: Spotify Launches
events.blurb: A Swedish music-streaming service, developed in Stockholm and Stockholm alone for two years, launched invitation-only to users in six European countries. The service offered an enormous music library — eventually over 100 million tracks — free with ads or $10/month without. It would restructure the entire music business: album sales collapsed, streaming became the default, and royalties flowed through aggregation models that artists found miserly.
events.revealBlurb: October 7, 2008 — founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The service arrived in the U.S. in July 2011 after lengthy negotiations with major labels. It had 620 million monthly active users as of 2024 — the largest audio subscription service ever.

events.title: Battle of Bunker Hill
events.blurb: American militia who had occupied two hills on a peninsula north of Boston overnight were assaulted by British regulars advancing uphill in three waves. The defenders — reportedly told "don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" to conserve ammunition — inflicted heavy casualties on the first two waves before running out of powder and being driven from the ground. The British held the field but lost over 1,000 men; the American cause gained enormous moral prestige.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1775 — fought mostly on Breed's Hill; misnamed after the adjacent Bunker Hill. British commander: General Thomas Gage. American commander killed in the retreat: General Joseph Warren. Within days, Congress appointed George Washington commander-in-chief.

events.title: Storming of the Bastille
events.blurb: A mob of several thousand Parisians, enraged by the dismissal of a popular finance minister and rumours of royal military preparations, stormed a royal fortress prison on the city's eastern edge in search of gunpowder stored there. The garrison surrendered after a bloody four-hour assault; the commandant was murdered and his head carried on a pike through the streets. The prison itself held only seven prisoners. The date became the French national holiday.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1789 — the Bastille. Seven prisoners: four forgers, two lunatics, one aristocrat imprisoned by his family. Marquis de Launay, the commandant, is the famous head on the pike. Parisians began demolishing the fortress the next morning; it was fully down within three months.

events.title: Louis XVI Executed
events.blurb: A former French king, convicted by the National Convention of treason for allegedly conspiring with foreign powers against the revolution, was beheaded by a relatively new device on a Paris square as drums drowned out the opening lines of the speech he attempted to deliver from the scaffold. His wife, an Austrian-born former queen, would meet the same end nine months later. The regicide radicalized the revolution's enemies and internal fears alike.
events.revealBlurb: January 21, 1793 — Louis XVI at the Place de la Révolution (now Place de la Concorde). The National Convention had voted 361-360 for death, a margin of one. His final words were cut off by drums: "People, I die innocent..." Marie Antoinette was executed October 16, 1793.

events.title: Napoleon Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Corsican-born general, having ruled France as First Consul for five years, staged a coronation at the Gothic cathedral in the French capital. He had negotiated the pope's attendance; in the ceremony's most famous moment — possibly prearranged, possibly improvised — the emperor took the crown from the pope and placed it on his own head. The act was read as a message: no religious authority ratified his power.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1804 — Notre-Dame de Paris. Pope Pius VII had been brought from Rome; he sat largely passive through the ceremony. Napoleon's wife Joséphine also crowned herself empress. Jacques-Louis David's monumental painting of the coronation, finished three years later, flatters Napoleon's height among other details.

events.title: Battle of Leipzig
events.blurb: Four days of fighting around a Saxon city produced the largest battle in European history before World War I, with 600,000 men engaged. A coalition of Russian, Austrian, Prussian, and Swedish forces defeated Napoleon's Grand Army, pressuring a French retreat west over the Rhine. Napoleon had lost Germany; he would lose France within six months. The battle is known in Germany as the Battle of the Nations.
events.revealBlurb: October 16-19, 1813 — Leipzig, Saxony. Casualties: perhaps 100,000 total — roughly 38,000 French, 54,000 Allied. The Battle of Trafalgar eight years earlier had ended French naval power; Leipzig ended French land dominance.

events.title: Survivor Premieres
events.blurb: A CBS reality competition series premiered, dropping 16 Americans on a Malaysian island and instructing them to "outwit, outplay, outlast" each other in a game of voted-off eliminations for a million-dollar prize. The finale two months later drew 51 million viewers. The show's format — strangers in deprived conditions voting each other out week by week — launched the modern reality-TV boom and made "tribal council" a household phrase.
events.revealBlurb: May 31, 2000 — host Jeff Probst, season 1 winner Richard Hatch. Hatch was later convicted of tax evasion for failing to declare the million-dollar prize. The show has run 45 seasons as of 2024 and is still in production, a foundational text of unscripted American television.

events.title: Michael Jackson Dies
events.blurb: A 50-year-old American singer widely regarded as the most successful pop star of his generation died of cardiac arrest at his rented Los Angeles home while preparing for a 50-concert comeback tour in London. His personal physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter for administering propofol, a surgical anesthetic, to help him sleep. His death prompted an outpouring of grief that crashed major websites and sold over 35 million of his records in the following six months.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 2009 — Michael Jackson. His physician, Conrad Murray, was sentenced to 4 years and served 2. His public memorial on July 7 drew 31 million U.S. TV viewers. The "This Is It" concert film, compiled from rehearsal footage, grossed $261 million posthumously.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: Gangnam Style Goes Viral
events.blurb: A music video by a 34-year-old South Korean rapper was uploaded to YouTube, featuring a catchy synth-pop track, exaggerated dance moves, and satirical shots of an upscale Seoul district. Within three months the video had 300 million views, passing Justin Bieber's "Baby" as the most-viewed in YouTube history. Within five, it crossed one billion. The horse-riding dance broke through into American late-night comedy, political campaigns, and every wedding reception in the world.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 2012 — PSY (Park Jae-sang). It held the most-viewed YouTube video title until it was surpassed by "See You Again" in 2017 and then "Despacito." The video's 2014 view count literally broke YouTube's 32-bit counter, requiring an engineering upgrade to 64 bits.

events.title: Stranger Things Premieres
events.blurb: A supernatural drama set in a small Indiana town in 1983 premiered on Netflix, combining Spielbergian child adventure, Stephen King atmospheric horror, and 80s-movie production design with a pitch-perfect synth-wave score. The 8-episode first season was Netflix's first genuine original-production cultural sensation and proved that the streaming service could create prestige-TV hits without a traditional network. The cast of unknown child actors became overnight celebrities.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 2016 — Netflix; created by the Duffer Brothers. Cast included Winona Ryder, David Harbour, Millie Bobby Brown, Finn Wolfhard, Noah Schnapp. The 2022 season 4 episode "Running Up That Hill" pushed Kate Bush's 1985 single to #1 in the UK, 37 years after its original release.

events.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
events.blurb: At 7:55 that morning, 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft struck the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging 19 ships including eight battleships and destroying 188 aircraft in under two hours. The attack killed 2,403 Americans — including 1,177 sailors and Marines aboard the USS Arizona, which exploded catastrophically and sank in nine minutes.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1941 — Pearl Harbor, Oahu. The USS Arizona still lies on the harbor floor; approximately 900 of her crew remain entombed inside. The declaration of war passed Congress the next day, 470–1 — the single dissenting vote was from pacifist Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana.

events.title: Me 262's First All-Jet Flight
events.blurb: A swept-wing aircraft climbed away from a Bavarian airfield under pure jet power for the first time, reaching speeds that no piston-engined fighter could match, signalling that the era of propeller-driven military aviation was ending. The technology was real and available — but bureaucratic delays and a leadership obsession with bombers kept it from operational service for more than two years.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1942, Leipheim — pilot Fritz Wendel flew the Me 262 V3 on jet power alone for the first time. Hitler later insisted the aircraft be developed as a bomber rather than a fighter, reportedly costing Germany a 14-month delay. When it finally entered service in 1944, it was too little too late: fuel shortages kept most on the ground.

events.title: Allied Invasion of Sicily
events.blurb: The largest amphibious operation to that point in military history put 160,000 troops, 3,000 ships, and 4,000 aircraft onto a Mediterranean island in a single night and day — opening the Allied campaign on the European continent itself and within three weeks causing the arrest and removal of a dictator who had held power for two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 9–10, 1943 — Operation Husky. Benito Mussolini was deposed by his own Fascist Grand Council on July 25, just two weeks after the landings. An elaborate Allied deception operation, "Operation Mincemeat," had planted false documents on a corpse washed ashore in Spain suggesting the real target was Greece — and the Germans believed it.

events.title: Fall of Monte Cassino
events.blurb: After four separate offensives spanning five months, Polish troops raised their flag over the ruins of a hilltop monastery that had been reduced to rubble by an Allied bombing raid — finally cracking a mountain defensive line that had blocked the Allied advance up a peninsula for half a year and cost over 43,000 casualties across all the assaulting armies.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1944. Polish Corps commander General Anders had promised his men they would fight for Poland in the west since the Soviet Union had taken the east. Over 900 Polish soldiers died in the final assault. The monastery's Benedictine monks had evacuated its art treasures months earlier; the abbey itself was empty during the famous Allied bombing of February 15.

events.title: Trinity Atomic Test
events.blurb: Scientists detonated a plutonium device atop a 30-metre steel tower in a remote desert basin before dawn, producing a fireball seen 250 miles away, a shockwave felt 100 miles away, and a mushroom cloud rising 12 kilometres into the sky — proving that a new class of weapon with the destructive power of 18,600 tons of TNT was now a practical reality.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 1945 at 5:29:45 AM Mountain War Time, Jornada del Muerto desert, New Mexico. Witnessing the blast, project director J. Robert Oppenheimer recalled a line from the Bhagavad Gita: "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds." Test director Kenneth Bainbridge's assessment was more blunt: "Now we are all sons of bitches."

events.title: First Mars Close-Up Flyby
events.blurb: Mariner 4 flew within 9,846 km of Mars and transmitted 21 photographs covering about 1% of the planet's surface — the first close-range images of another planet. The images revealed a cratered, Moon-like landscape and showed Mars had a much thinner atmosphere than expected, with a surface pressure of roughly 4–7 millibars, dashing hopes of a habitable world.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1965 — Mariner 4. The images took four days to receive and were so eagerly anticipated that JPL technicians printed the first strips of data by hand onto paper using artist's pastels, coloring by number before the computer could process the file. The result was a blurry colored rectangle they pinned to a bulletin board.

events.title: Lunar Surface Landing
events.blurb: A spacecraft descended onto the Sea of Tranquility with 25 seconds of fuel remaining after the landing computer triggered five 1202 alarms caused by executive overflow. Two crew members spent 2 hours 31 minutes on the surface, collecting 21.5 kg of rock and soil and deploying a seismometer and a retroreflector array.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Apollo 11. Armstrong's first step came at 10:56 PM Eastern. The descent stage still sits on the Moon; the flag was knocked flat by the liftoff exhaust. The line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — the transmission dropped the article, and Armstrong spent decades insisting he said it.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: First Orbital Rocket Booster Landing
events.blurb: A SpaceX Falcon 9 first stage returned from an orbital-class mission and landed upright at Landing Zone 1 in Cape Canaveral, completing the first successful recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster under propulsive control. The same vehicle had delivered 11 commercial satellites to orbit minutes earlier and touched down within about 10 meters of the target pad.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2015 — OG-2 Mission 2. SpaceX had attempted and failed four previous booster landings on a drone ship at sea. The Falcon's legs deployed at 180 m altitude. Elon Musk posted one word after confirmation: "Welcome back, baby." The reused booster concept cut launch costs by roughly 30%.

events.title: First South Pole Moon Landing
events.blurb: India's Chandrayaan-3 Vikram lander set down at 69°S latitude near the lunar south pole — the highest-latitude soft landing on the Moon ever achieved — just days after a Russian Luna-25 mission attempting the same target crashed on approach. The Pragyan rover confirmed the presence of sulfur, oxygen, iron, and other elements in the regolith through laser spectroscopy.
events.revealBlurb: August 23, 2023 — Chandrayaan-3. The mission cost approximately $75 million — cheaper than many Hollywood blockbusters and a fraction of comparable NASA missions. India became only the fourth nation to soft-land on the Moon and the first to reach the south polar region. The rover covered 100 meters before being placed in sleep mode ahead of the lunar night; it did not wake up.

events.title: Gallic Sack of Rome
events.blurb: Senone Gauls under their chieftain Brennus routed a Roman army at the Allia River, then entered a largely deserted Rome three days later and burned it for seven months. The sole holdout was the Capitoline Hill, where a sacred flock of geese allegedly woke the defenders when a Gallic night-assault crept up the cliffs.
events.revealBlurb: July 390 BCE, traditional (Polybius says 387). The ransom Brennus demanded in gold was agreed, but the Romans protested he was using rigged weights. Brennus reportedly threw his sword onto the scales and bellowed "Vae victis" — "Woe to the vanquished."

events.title: The First Triumvirate
events.blurb: Julius Caesar secretly brokered a private political alliance with Rome's two most powerful men: Gnaeus Pompey, celebrated general of the East, and Marcus Crassus, the wealthiest man in Roman history. The three agreed to combine their networks and veto power to dominate legislation; the alliance had no legal standing, no name, and no public announcement.
events.revealBlurb: Late 60 BCE, Rome. Crassus, reportedly worth 200 million sesterces, once claimed no man was truly rich unless he could afford to maintain an army from his own pocket. He would later die at the Battle of Carrhae when, according to legend, the Parthians poured molten gold down his throat.

events.title: Great Fire of Rome
events.blurb: A fire that broke out near the Circus Maximus burned for nine days and destroyed or severely damaged ten of Rome's fourteen districts, leaving the majority of the population homeless. Emperor Nero, who was at Antium when the fire started, blamed the city's small Christian community and launched the first state-sanctioned persecution of Christians in Roman history.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 64 CE. The story that Nero fiddled while Rome burned is almost certainly false — the fiddle didn't exist yet, and multiple sources place him outside the city at the time. Tacitus, writing fifty years later, noted that many Romans suspected Nero ordered the fire himself but that the charge was never proven.

events.title: Caracalla's Citizenship Edict
events.blurb: Emperor Caracalla issued a decree granting full Roman citizenship to every free person throughout the empire, erasing a 700-year distinction between citizen and non-citizen that had shaped Roman law, military service, and taxation. Modern historians debate whether the primary motive was ideological universalism or a straightforward need to expand the tax base.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 212 CE. Caracalla's full name — Marcus Aurelius Severus Antoninus — was a collection of borrowed dynastic brands. "Caracalla" was the nickname Romans gave him, after a Gallic hooded cloak he popularised. He had his brother and co-emperor Geta killed months before signing this edict.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: Trinity Nuclear Test
events.blurb: A plutonium implosion device was detonated atop a 30-metre steel tower in the New Mexico desert, producing a fireball visible 160 kilometres away and an explosion equivalent to 21 kilotons of TNT. Watching from a bunker 16 kilometres distant, the project's scientific director later recalled a verse from Hindu scripture about becoming death, destroyer of worlds.

events.title: People's Republic of China Proclaimed
events.blurb: Standing above a vast plaza in the Chinese capital, a revolutionary leader announced the founding of a new communist state after two decades of civil war and foreign occupation. His defeated nationalist rival retreated to an island 160 kilometres off the mainland coast and established a rival regime that persists today.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1949 — Mao Zedong declared the PRC from the Tiananmen gate. Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan with 2 million refugees and most of the mainland's gold reserves. The split still defines East Asian geopolitics.

events.title: Gulf of Tonkin Incident
events.blurb: A U.S. Navy destroyer reported it had been attacked by small torpedo boats off the North Vietnamese coast. Two nights later, the same destroyer and a second reported a second attack in bad weather — an attack that likely never happened. Within days, Congress passed a resolution authorizing the president to use "all necessary measures" in Southeast Asia, opening the door to full-scale war.
events.revealBlurb: August 2 and 4, 1964 — the second "attack" was almost certainly radar ghosts and jumpy sonar operators. The resolution passed the House 416-0 and the Senate 88-2. Declassified NSA documents in 2005 confirmed the fabrication.

events.title: Moscow Olympics Boycott
events.blurb: Sixty-six nations, led by the United States, refused to send athletes to the Summer Games held in the Soviet capital, protesting the invasion of a neighboring country five months earlier. Eighty nations competed anyway — the smallest field since 1956. Four years later, the Soviet bloc returned the favor by boycotting the Los Angeles Games.
events.revealBlurb: July 19, 1980 — the boycott was announced by Jimmy Carter. British athletes defied their own government and competed under the Olympic flag. The 1984 Soviet retaliation cost American sprinter Evelyn Ashford a likely gold-medal duel.

events.title: Romanian Revolution
events.blurb: Within ten days, a dictator who had ruled a Balkan nation for 24 years lost control of a mass demonstration, fled the capital by helicopter, was captured, given a two-hour military tribunal, and executed by firing squad on Christmas Day alongside his wife. It was the only violent collapse among the eastern bloc regimes that fell at the time.
events.revealBlurb: December 16-25, 1989 — Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu. Soldiers actually had to be ordered to stop shooting them — they kept firing at the already-dead bodies. Ceaușescu's final request was to sing the Internationale. It was denied.

events.title: British Parliament Passes the Stamp Act
events.blurb: Parliament enacted a sweeping tax requiring colonists to purchase revenue stamps for newspapers, legal documents, almanacs, and even playing cards — the first direct tax Britain had ever levied on its American colonies. Outcry was immediate and visceral: colonial assemblies passed resolutions of protest, merchants organized boycotts, and a new network of radicals calling themselves the Sons of Liberty took to the streets.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1765 — London. The tax was repealed the following year under merchant pressure, but Parliament simultaneously passed the Declaratory Act asserting its absolute right to tax the colonies "in all cases whatsoever." The colonists celebrated the repeal and mostly ignored the Declaratory Act — for about a decade.

events.title: Alien and Sedition Acts Signed
events.blurb: President John Adams signed four statutes that extended the residency requirement for citizenship from five to fourteen years, empowered the president to expel foreigners deemed dangerous, and made it a crime to publish "false, scandalous, and malicious" criticism of the government. The laws were aimed largely at French immigrants and Republican newspaper editors who opposed the Federalist administration.
events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1798 — Philadelphia (the Sedition Act, last of the four). Twenty-five people were arrested and ten convicted under the Sedition Act — all of them Jefferson's supporters. Jefferson himself quietly wrote the Kentucky Resolutions arguing states could nullify federal law.

events.title: Women's Suffrage Amendment Certified
events.blurb: The U.S. Secretary of State certified the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment, prohibiting any state from denying the right to vote on account of sex. The amendment's passage followed a 72-year organised campaign that had begun at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848, when most of its original signatories were ridiculed for the demand.

events.title: Apollo 11: First Humans on the Moon
events.blurb: At 10:56 pm EDT that evening, astronaut Neil Armstrong stepped off the lunar module Eagle onto the surface of the Moon and became the first human being to walk on another world, watched live by an estimated 600 million people — roughly one-fifth of humanity. Buzz Aldrin joined him 19 minutes later; the two planted an American flag, collected samples, and departed after 2 hours and 31 minutes on the surface.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Sea of Tranquility, the Moon. Armstrong's famous line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — he swears he said it; the transmission dropped the "a." Michael Collins orbited alone overhead for 21 hours while his crewmates were on the surface. President Nixon had a speechwriter prepare a statement in case they didn't make it back.

events.title: Bush v. Gore Halts Florida Recount
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 to halt the manual recount of Florida's contested presidential ballots, effectively awarding the state's 25 electoral votes to Republican George W. Bush and deciding the closest presidential election since 1876. The margin in Florida's certified count was 537 votes out of nearly 6 million cast; Al Gore ultimately conceded, and Bush won the presidency 271–266 in the Electoral College.
events.revealBlurb: December 12, 2000 — Washington, D.C. The per curiam opinion included the extraordinary disclaimer that the ruling "is limited to the present circumstances" and should not be treated as precedent. The butterfly ballot design in Palm Beach County alone may have cost Gore 2,000–3,000 votes to Pat Buchanan.

events.title: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre
events.blurb: A British brigadier-general marched 50 rifle-armed soldiers into a walled garden in a Punjabi city where thousands of Sikhs, Hindus, and Muslims had gathered for a spring harvest festival. Without warning, he ordered ten minutes of continuous fire into the unarmed crowd, ceasing only when ammunition ran low. Official counts put the dead at 379; Indian sources gave over 1,000. He was celebrated in parts of British society as a saviour of empire.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1919 — Amritsar, Baisakhi day. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer. The poet Rabindranath Tagore renounced his British knighthood in protest. A young Sikh named Udham Singh, who was at the garden that day, assassinated the former lieutenant-governor responsible for the region 21 years later in London.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Economic Liberalization
events.blurb: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis so acute that the country had airlifted 47 tonnes of its gold reserves to London as collateral, a new finance minister presented a budget that systematically dismantled the license-permit-quota economy that had governed Indian business for four decades. Industrial licensing was abolished, imports liberalized, foreign investment welcomed. The economy would nearly quintuple over the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: July 24, 1991 — Finance Minister Manmohan Singh's budget speech. Prime Minister Narasimha Rao provided the political cover. Singh, invoking Victor Hugo, declared: "No power on Earth can stop an idea whose time has come."

events.title: Pokhran-II Nuclear Tests
events.blurb: India conducted five underground nuclear explosions over two days in the same Rajasthani desert test range it had used 24 years earlier, including a claimed thermonuclear device. The tests, carried out in conditions of extraordinary operational security that surprised American intelligence satellites, declared the country a full nuclear-weapon state. Pakistan tested its own devices 17 days later.
events.revealBlurb: May 11 and 13, 1998 — code-named Operation Shakti. Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee had been in office three months. Sanctions were imposed; they were lifted within two years as the United States reassessed its South Asia policy.

events.title: Kargil War
events.blurb: Pakistani soldiers, disguised as local insurgents, occupied high-altitude ridges inside the Indian-administered portion of a disputed northern territory over the winter. Their discovery by a shepherd in early May touched off a 74-day war fought at elevations up to 5,600 metres. India retook the peaks one by one with heavy infantry losses; Pakistan, pressured by Washington, withdrew.
events.revealBlurb: May 3 to July 26, 1999 — the Line of Control in Kargil, Ladakh. The conflict was one of the first televised wars in India. Captain Vikram Batra became a national hero before dying on Point 4875 on July 7.

events.title: Machu Picchu Built
events.blurb: An Inca emperor's royal estate was built at 2,430 metres on a narrow mountain ridge above a river in the Andes, with 200 stone buildings — agricultural terraces, palaces, temples — arranged on a mountain site that seemed intended for dramatic rather than practical reasons. It was abandoned roughly a century later for unclear reasons, possibly connected to the Spanish conquest of the Inca. The site remained unknown to the Spanish and, largely, to the outside world until 1911.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1450 — emperor Pachacuti. The American explorer Hiram Bingham encountered it on July 24, 1911. Local farmers had never really forgotten it; the "rediscovery" was primarily for outside audiences. It is now one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

events.title: US Capitol Cornerstone Laid
events.blurb: The president of the newly independent United States — wearing a Masonic apron — laid the cornerstone of a new federal capitol building on a wooded hill above the banks of the Potomac River. The building was meant to house the U.S. Congress. The winning design, by a Scottish-trained amateur architect, was a neoclassical rotunda crowned with a low dome; later architects would replace the dome with a much taller cast-iron one during the Civil War.
events.revealBlurb: September 18, 1793 — George Washington at Jenkins Hill (now Capitol Hill), Washington, D.C. Designer: William Thornton. The current wedding-cake dome was built 1855-1866 by Thomas U. Walter and crowned with the Statue of Freedom during the Civil War. Slave labour built much of the original building.

events.title: Sagrada Família Begun
