events.blurb: Construction began on a Catholic basilica in the Catalan capital, funded by donations alone — a condition that would stretch the project across a century and a half. The original architect was replaced after one year by a 31-year-old ferociously religious designer who would pour the rest of his life into the project, combining Gothic and Art Nouveau influences into a style of his own. He would die 43 years later, hit by a tram on the street outside; only a fraction of the church was finished. Construction continues today.
events.revealBlurb: March 19, 1882 — original architect Francisco de Paula del Villar; succeeded 1883 by Antoni Gaudí. Gaudí devoted the last 15 years of his life exclusively to the project. He was hit by a tram on June 7, 1926; his grave is in the crypt. Completion is projected for 2026 — a century after his death.

events.title: Statue of Liberty Dedicated
events.blurb: A 46-metre-tall copper statue of a robed woman holding a torch, a gift from the French people commemorating American independence (with an eye toward French republican aspirations), was dedicated on a small island in New York Harbor in the rain. It had been designed by a French sculptor, its internal iron framework engineered by the man who would five years later design a certain Paris tower, and shipped across the Atlantic in 350 pieces.
events.revealBlurb: October 28, 1886 — sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi; engineer Gustave Eiffel. The statue was meant to arrive for the 1876 centennial; it missed by a decade due to fundraising troubles. The poem on its pedestal ("Give me your tired, your poor...") was added in 1903 from a sonnet by Emma Lazarus.

events.title: Channel Tunnel Opens
events.blurb: A 50-kilometre twin-bore railway tunnel under the English Channel opened, linking France to Britain below the sea floor for the first time in 8,000 years. The tunnel had been proposed repeatedly since the early 19th century but had always been shelved on defensive grounds; the end of the Cold War and European integration finally made it buildable. Construction had involved eleven tunnel-boring machines drilling simultaneously from both sides; the breakthrough was within 35 centimetres alignment.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1994 — Queen Elizabeth II and President François Mitterrand cut a ribbon jointly. Total project cost: £9 billion, roughly 80 percent over budget. The tunnel is used by Eurostar passenger trains and the freight-carrying Shuttle. Trains reach 160 km/h underground.

events.title: Great Exhibition Opens
events.blurb: Queen Victoria opened a five-month international exhibition of industrial and artistic products housed in a vast prefabricated iron-and-glass structure in Hyde Park — the building nicknamed the "Crystal Palace." 14,000 exhibitors from 25 countries displayed 100,000 exhibits; six million visitors paid admission. The exhibition's organizer, Prince Albert, had intended it as both a celebration of industrial progress and a showcase for the superiority of free trade. It made a healthy profit, used to found London museums.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1851 — Prince Albert's Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations. Designer Joseph Paxton, a gardener turned architect, had designed the building in a single afternoon on a sheet of blotting paper. The profit funded the Victoria and Albert, Science, and Natural History museums.

events.title: Transatlantic Telegraph Cable Completed
events.blurb: The steamship Great Eastern finished laying 4,000 kilometres of insulated copper wire across the floor of the Atlantic, connecting Valencia Island, Ireland, to Heart's Content, Newfoundland. The first commercial message crossed in minutes — a journey that had previously taken ten days by ship.

events.title: Coca-Cola Invented
events.blurb: An Atlanta pharmacist, a former Confederate officer who had become addicted to morphine following a Civil War injury, mixed a flavoured syrup of coca leaves and kola nuts with carbonated water at a downtown soda fountain and began selling it by the glass as a "brain tonic." The formula initially contained a small amount of cocaine; it was removed in 1903. The modestly popular local beverage grew into the world's most recognized consumer brand.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1886 — John Pemberton at Jacobs' Pharmacy, Atlanta. Pemberton sold the formula piecemeal in ill health; Asa Griggs Candler consolidated ownership and built the business. Coca-Cola's secret recipe, "Merchandise 7X," is supposedly known to only two executives at any time.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Homestead Strike
events.blurb: A Pennsylvania steelworkers' strike against wage cuts at a mill owned by a famous industrialist turned into a gun battle after management hired 300 Pinkerton private detectives to escort strike-breakers into the plant. The Pinkertons arrived by barge up the Monongahela River before dawn; strikers and their families met them on the banks with rifles. Nine strikers and seven Pinkertons died in the all-day firefight. The state militia restored order; the union was broken; US steelworkers remained largely non-unionized for 45 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 1892 — Homestead Steel Works, owned by Andrew Carnegie, managed during the strike by Henry Clay Frick. Frick survived an assassination attempt by anarchist Alexander Berkman three weeks later, shot and stabbed multiple times but recovered. Carnegie was in Scotland when the violence occurred.

events.title: Asteroids Released by Atari
events.blurb: Drawing lines on a vector monitor to simulate drifting through space debris sounds modest. The game that resulted became Atari's best-selling arcade cabinet of all time, pulling in an estimated 10 million quarters per day at its peak. Demand was so extreme that Atari temporarily halted production of other games and shipped Asteroids units inside Lunar Lander cabinets just to get them out the door faster.
events.revealBlurb: November 1979 — Atari released Asteroids in North American arcades. It sold over 70,000 cabinets. The game's high score table was the first widely adopted public performance metric in gaming — and the first subject of documented high-score fraud.

events.title: Pac-Man Debuts in Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: A yellow circle eating dots and fleeing ghosts through a maze seemed like a peculiar bet in an era dominated by shoot-'em-ups. It became the highest-grossing arcade game ever made, the first video game character to achieve mass-market celebrity, and the template for an entirely new genre. Its creator wanted a game that women would actually want to play.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1980 — Namco's Puck-Man (renamed Pac-Man for Western markets to prevent vandalism) went on location test in Shibuya, Tokyo. By 1982 an estimated 30 billion quarters had been inserted into Pac-Man machines worldwide.

events.title: Nintendo Famicom Launches in Japan
events.blurb: A cheap red-and-white 8-bit console hit Japanese shelves the same day as a competing machine. Within a year it had outsold every rival combined, driven fourteen manufacturers out of the market entirely, and established Nintendo as the unchallenged ruler of the Japanese gaming business.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1983 — Nintendo's Family Computer launched in Japan at ¥14,800, head-to-head with Sega's SG-1000. The NES version launched in New York in October 1985. The NES/Famicom line sold 61.91 million units worldwide.

events.title: Nintendo Game Boy Launches in North America
events.blurb: Competing handhelds boasted colour screens and better hardware. Nintendo shipped a grey brick with a pea-green LCD and bundled it with a Soviet puzzle game about falling tetrominoes. The grey brick won. Within weeks every unit in the United States had sold out.
events.revealBlurb: July 31, 1989 — The Game Boy launched in North America at $89.99, selling 40,000 units on day one. The Game Boy line eventually sold 118 million units. The Japan launch had been April 21, 1989.

events.title: League of Legends Launches
events.blurb: A free-to-play adaptation of a Warcraft III fan modification launched quietly and grew into the most-played PC game on Earth. At its peak over 100 million accounts had been registered, and its annual World Championship filled football stadiums and drew broadcast audiences that dwarfed traditional sporting events. It invented a new genre name — MOBA — and made esports a career path.
events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Intel Founded
events.blurb: Two former engineers from a Silicon Valley semiconductor firm incorporated a new company — named by combining "integrated" and "electronics" — to build memory chips. They raised $2.5 million in three days by phoning Arthur Rock, a venture capitalist. Their first memory product sold poorly; a side project to build a calculator chip would, three years later, lead them to invent the microprocessor and change the direction of the industry.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1968 — Gordon Moore and Robert Noyce. Their early employees included Andy Grove, later to become Intel's famously paranoid CEO. The name "Intel" had been claimed by a hotel chain; they paid $15,000 for the trademark.

events.title: Apple II Released
events.blurb: A young Californian computer company released their second machine — and the first mass-market personal computer designed for non-hobbyists, with built-in color graphics, a working keyboard, a plastic case, and the ability to display text and graphics simultaneously. It shipped for $1,298 and found a broad market among small businesses, schools, and households. Apple's revenues grew 700 percent a year for five consecutive years.
events.revealBlurb: June 10, 1977 — Apple Computer. Engineered largely by Steve Wozniak. The arrival of VisiCalc two years later made it the first computer that small businesses felt they had to buy. Apple sold over 5 million Apple IIs before discontinuing the line in 1993.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: iPod Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a white portable music player with a 5 GB hard drive — "1,000 songs in your pocket," according to its co-founder's introduction — and a scrollwheel for navigation. The industry press was unimpressed; smaller MP3 players already existed. Over the next decade, the iPod and its derivatives would sell over 400 million units, reshape the music industry, and serve as a forerunner and technological foundation for the iPhone.
events.revealBlurb: October 23, 2001 — Apple iPod. Steve Jobs introduced it at a small press event, not to a large keynote crowd. Initial reviews focused on how it was Mac-only; the 2003 Windows version opened the floodgates.

events.title: First Android Phone Released
events.blurb: A Taiwanese handset maker released the first commercial phone running an open-source mobile operating system developed by a Silicon Valley search-engine company, available through a US mobile carrier. The device had a physical keyboard that slid out from under the screen; unlike the rival iPhone, users could install apps from anywhere, replace the default apps, and generally modify the device at will. Open-ecosystem Android would grow to dominate global smartphone market share.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 2008 — T-Mobile G1 (HTC Dream), running Android 1.0. Google had quietly acquired Android Inc. for $50 million in 2005. By 2013 more than half of smartphones sold ran Android; today it's over 70 percent globally.

events.title: Jackie Robinson Breaks Color Barrier
events.blurb: A 28-year-old second baseman took the field at a Brooklyn ballpark and became the first African-American to play in modern Major League Baseball, breaking a 63-year color line enforced by gentlemen's agreement rather than written rule. He went hitless in his debut but reached base on an error and scored the winning run.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1947 — Ebbets Field, Brooklyn Dodgers. Team president Branch Rickey had signed him with the understanding he would absorb abuse without retaliation for two years. Robinson's number 42 was retired across every MLB team in 1997, the only such universal retirement in sports.

events.title: Military Desegregation Order
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed an executive order mandating "equality of treatment and opportunity" in the armed forces without regard to race, color, religion, or national origin. The army resisted for nearly five years; full integration of combat units was not achieved until the Korean War made ignoring Black replacements impossible.
events.revealBlurb: July 26, 1948 — Executive Order 9981, Harry Truman. He signed it partly out of conviction, partly because Black voters in northern cities were now pivotal to Democratic victory. The last all-Black unit was dissolved in 1954.

events.title: Greensboro Sit-Ins
events.blurb: Four Black college freshmen sat down at the segregated lunch counter of a downtown variety store in a North Carolina city and politely ordered coffee. When refused service, they stayed seated until closing. They returned the next day with more students. Within two months, similar sit-ins had spread to 55 cities in 13 states, and the variety-store chain desegregated its counters.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 1960 — Woolworth's lunch counter, Greensboro. The original four were students at North Carolina A&T State University: Ezell Blair, Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil, David Richmond. Part of the counter is now in the Smithsonian.

events.title: Bloody Sunday in Selma
events.blurb: Six hundred civil-rights marchers, demanding federal protection for Black voting rights, set out from a small Alabama city to walk 87 kilometres to the state capital. On the Edmund Pettus Bridge at the edge of town, state troopers and a sheriff's posse on horseback charged them with clubs and tear gas. Televised images of a beaten John Lewis shocked the nation into action.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1965 — Selma, Alabama. Lewis's skull was fractured. Lyndon Johnson appeared before a joint session of Congress eight days later to introduce the Voting Rights Act, closing with the movement's own anthem: "We shall overcome."

events.title: MLK Day Signed
events.blurb: After 15 years of advocacy by civil rights leaders, Congress passed and the president signed legislation establishing the third Monday of January as a federal holiday honoring the slain civil rights leader. The fight to pass it had drawn bitter opposition from some senators, including one who conducted a 16-day filibuster. It became the first federal holiday commemorating an African-American.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 1983 — Ronald Reagan. Arizona voters rejected recognizing the holiday in 1990; the NFL moved the 1993 Super Bowl from Phoenix in response, and the state reversed course. New Hampshire, the last holdout, adopted it in 1999.

events.title: McCarthy Wheeling Speech
events.blurb: At a Lincoln Day dinner in West Virginia, a previously obscure U.S. senator brandished a piece of paper and claimed it listed 205 known communists working in the State Department. The charge, later revised repeatedly and never substantiated, launched a four-year domestic witch-hunt that would bear his name.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1950 — Joseph McCarthy, up for re-election, stumbled onto his signature issue. The "list" he waved kept changing: 205, then 57, then 81. No copy of the original was ever produced. It destroyed thousands of careers anyway.

events.title: Korean War Armistice
events.blurb: After three years and more than two million deaths, military commanders from three nations signed a ceasefire in a frontier village, establishing a 4-kilometre-wide demilitarized strip along the 38th parallel where fighting had essentially started. No peace treaty has ever been signed. The two Koreas remain technically at war.
events.revealBlurb: July 27, 1953 — signed at Panmunjom. The DMZ is now the most heavily mined place on Earth. Because no peace treaty followed, a single gunshot across the line could theoretically restart the war tomorrow.

events.title: Kitchen Debate
events.blurb: At the opening of an American National Exhibition in Moscow, a U.S. vice president and a Soviet premier stood beside a model suburban kitchen and argued about consumer goods, nuclear weapons, and the relative virtues of their systems. Live cameras caught every jabbing finger. Polaroid prints of the exchange appeared in American newspapers within days.
events.revealBlurb: July 24, 1959 — Richard Nixon and Nikita Khrushchev at Sokolniki Park. The kitchen was a General Electric display. Nixon's ability to hold his own in the unscripted shouting match boosted his 1960 presidential prospects (though not quite enough).

events.title: Berlin Wall Built
events.blurb: Overnight, East German soldiers and workers unrolled barbed wire along the jagged frontier between the two halves of a divided city, cutting off the escape route that some 3.5 million people had used to flee west over the previous twelve years. Within days the wire was replaced with concrete. Families woke to find themselves permanently separated from relatives one street away.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1961 — construction began at 2 AM on a Sunday. The wall eventually grew to 155 kilometres, with 302 watchtowers and a "death strip" of raked sand and trip-wires. At least 140 people died trying to cross it going west.

events.title: Solidarity Founded
events.blurb: A strike at a shipyard in a Polish coastal city, led by an electrician who had been fired for union organizing, forced the communist government to sign an agreement permitting an independent, self-governing trade union — the first in the eastern bloc. Within a year ten million workers had joined. Martial law followed in December 1981, but the genie was out.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1980 — the Gdańsk Agreement. Electrician Lech Wałęsa would win the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983 and become Poland's first post-communist president in 1990. The movement's red logo, hand-painted in a shipyard, became an icon.

events.title: Tangshan Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.6 earthquake struck a heavily industrialized city in northern China at 3:42 AM, when residents were asleep in masonry buildings that collapsed upon them. Official Chinese figures put the death toll at 242,000, but some estimates exceed 650,000. It is the second-deadliest earthquake of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: July 28, 1976 — Tangshan, Hebei Province. Mao Zedong, dying in Beijing, was briefly informed and reportedly wept. He died six weeks later; many traditional Chinese interpreters saw the quake as the Mandate of Heaven being withdrawn from his regime.

events.title: Deepwater Horizon Spill
events.blurb: A blowout on a semi-submersible drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico killed 11 workers and severed the riser pipe to a well 1,500 metres below the surface. Over the next 87 days, as engineers tried increasingly improbable methods to cap it, roughly 780 million litres of crude oil gushed into the sea — the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 2010 — off Louisiana. The well was finally killed in mid-September. BP paid over $65 billion in settlements, fines, and cleanup. A live-stream of the ocean-floor plume was watched by millions during the crisis; executives who claimed it was "relatively tiny" became memes.

events.title: Black Summer Bushfires
events.blurb: A prolonged drought and record heat fueled a six-month season of bushfires that burned 24 million hectares of southeastern Australia — an area larger than England. 33 people died directly; several hundred more from smoke. An estimated one billion wild animals perished. Smoke drifted across the Pacific and circled the globe.
events.revealBlurb: September 2019 – March 2020 — Australia. Images of koalas drinking from cyclists' water bottles and a town sheltering under blood-red skies went viral. Firefighters came from 12 countries. The season ended just as COVID-19 lockdowns began, compounding public trauma.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Declared
events.blurb: The World Health Organization, having watched a novel coronavirus spread from a single city to 114 countries in ten weeks, formally upgraded its assessment from epidemic to pandemic. Within days, much of the world entered some form of lockdown — schools shut, flights grounded, stock markets crashed. Before vaccines arrived a year later, it would kill millions.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2020 — WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. The first known case had been reported in Wuhan in early December 2019. Official global death toll exceeded 7 million; excess mortality studies suggest the real number is closer to 20 million.

events.title: Beirut Port Explosion
events.blurb: 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate that had been haphazardly stored in a warehouse at a Mediterranean capital's port for six years detonated after a smaller fire reached it. The blast was felt 240 kilometres away in Cyprus, killed 218 people, injured 7,000, and left 300,000 homeless. It ranks among the largest non-nuclear explosions ever recorded.
events.revealBlurb: August 4, 2020 — Beirut, Lebanon. The chemicals had been offloaded from a Russian ship in 2013 and simply abandoned. The blast crater was 124 metres wide. Years later no senior official has faced trial; the investigation has been repeatedly obstructed by politicians named as suspects.

events.title: MTV First Broadcast
events.blurb: A music video channel began broadcasting at 12:01 a.m., opening with a brief spoken introduction before playing a three-minute clip of a rock band performing against footage of a rocket launch. The first words spoken on air were "Ladies and gentlemen, rock and roll" — the channel ran continuously for 24 hours with no advertisements.

events.title: Rubik's Cube Global Craze
events.blurb: A 3×3 mechanical puzzle cube invented six years earlier by a Hungarian architecture professor became a global bestseller after licensed international distribution began. Over 100 million units sold in the first three years. Books of solutions appeared on bestseller lists. The puzzle's simplicity — six colours, 43 quintillion possible states, a single solved configuration — caught people who had never bought a toy in their lives. World championships began in 1982.
events.revealBlurb: 1981 — Ernő Rubik had patented the cube in 1975; it went international in 1980. The first world championship was in Budapest, June 5, 1982; the current world record for solving it is under 3.05 seconds (Max Park, June 2023). The cube remains in continuous production.

events.title: Prince Charles Marries Diana
events.blurb: The heir to the British throne, 32, married a 20-year-old shy nursery-school assistant at a grand ceremony at a London cathedral. The televised wedding drew 750 million viewers worldwide and unfolded like a fairytale: horse-drawn carriages, a 25-foot train on the bride's silk ivory dress, a balcony kiss at a royal palace afterward. The marriage itself would be miserable; the couple separated in 1992 and divorced in 1996. Both remarried others, and the bride died in a Paris car crash in 1997.
events.revealBlurb: July 29, 1981 — Charles, Prince of Wales and Lady Diana Spencer at St. Paul's Cathedral. Diana tripped on her father's name during the vows ("Philip Charles Arthur George" instead of "Charles Philip..."). Charles, now King Charles III, succeeded his mother Elizabeth II in September 2022.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: Peloponnesian War Begins
events.blurb: Tensions between a democratic maritime empire led by Athens and an aristocratic land-based league led by Sparta erupted into open war when Spartan forces invaded Athenian-allied territory. The war would last 27 years, consume Greek wealth, shatter Athenian power, and undermine Greek confidence in the democratic project. A historian who had commanded an Athenian force early in the war produced a narrative account considered a founding masterpiece of Western historiography.
events.revealBlurb: 431 BCE — Athens vs. Sparta. The historian was Thucydides. A plague in 430 BCE killed perhaps a quarter of the Athenian population, including the city's leader Pericles. Athens finally surrendered in 404 BCE after its fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami; Socrates was executed in Athens five years later.

events.title: Battle of Chaeronea
events.blurb: A Macedonian king's army of 32,000 defeated a combined Athenian-Theban force of similar size in central Greece, ending the independence of the classical Greek city-states. The victor's 18-year-old son, commanding the Macedonian left wing, personally broke the famous Sacred Band of Thebes — a unit of 300 elite warrior-lovers who died to the man. The defeat of the city-states unified Greece under Macedonian hegemony and set up the Asian conquests that would follow.
events.revealBlurb: August 338 BCE — King Philip II and his son Alexander. The Sacred Band of Thebes had won every battle it had fought for 40 years; it lost only at Chaeronea. Philip erected a stone lion over their mass grave; the lion, damaged over millennia, was restored in 1902 and still stands there.

events.title: Battle of Cannae
events.blurb: Hannibal's army of roughly 50,000 men destroyed a Roman force of 80,000 in a single afternoon by letting the Roman center push forward into a concave line, then closing cavalry on both flanks until the entire legionary mass was encircled and butchered. Between 55,000 and 70,000 Romans died; senators threw handfuls of gold rings stripped from dead equestrians into a bowl to show Carthage the scale of the slaughter.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 216 BCE, Apulia. The double-envelopment Hannibal used at Cannae became the template studied at military academies for 2,000 years. Hannibal's war elephants, his most famous asset, had all died before this battle.

events.title: Julius Caesar Assassinated
events.blurb: A Roman dictator, having been named dictator-for-life a month earlier, was stabbed 23 times by a group of 60 senators at a meeting of the Senate held in a Pompey-built theatre. The assassins, styling themselves "Liberators," had convinced themselves that removing the man who had effectively ended the Republic would restore it. Instead, his death plunged Rome into 14 more years of civil war, at the end of which his adopted heir emerged as the first Roman emperor in all but name.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 44 BCE — the Ides of March. Conspirators included Brutus and Cassius. The supposed last words "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare; Caesar's actual last words — if he spoke any — may have been the Greek "kai su, teknon?" ("you too, my child?"). His heir Octavian defeated the conspirators at Philippi two years later.

events.title: Destruction of the Second Temple
events.blurb: A Roman general's army of 70,000 legionaries, closing the siege of a rebellious Judean capital after a four-year Jewish revolt, breached the walls and burned the city's Second Temple on the anniversary of the first Temple's destruction 656 years earlier. The Temple was never rebuilt; a Western retaining wall remains the holiest site in Judaism. Roman troops hauled the Temple menorah and other sacred vessels to Rome, where a victory arch depicting the procession still stands.
events.revealBlurb: 70 CE — the siege was commanded by Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian. The Arch of Titus, completed c. 81 CE, still stands at the east end of the Roman Forum. The Western Wall is the most significant surviving fragment; Orthodox Jews mourn the Temple's destruction each year on Tisha B'Av.

events.title: Mother India Released
events.blurb: A near-three-hour epic about a village woman who spends decades breaking stones, raising sons, and protecting her community from a money-lender opened on Diwali across India and broke every box-office record to that point. The following year it became India's first film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film — losing by a single vote to a Federico Fellini picture.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1957. Directed by Mehboob Khan. Nargis, who plays the mother, married co-star Sunil Dutt after he dragged her unconscious from a fire that broke out on set. Khan's production logo featured a hammer-and-sickle; it was quietly removed before the Oscar submission print.

events.title: Mughal-e-Azam Released
events.blurb: A Mughal-court epic that took sixteen years to complete — halted twice by financial collapse and partitioned away from its original cast — cost ₹1.5 crore, more than any previous Indian film, and spent ₹1 crore on a single song filmed in a replica of the Sheesh Mahal built with imported Belgian glass. Released in black and white, it was the highest-grossing Indian film for fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1960 — directed by K. Asif. The original Akbar died before filming could restart; the entire cast was rebuilt after Partition. In 2004 it became the first Indian black-and-white film to be digitally colourised and theatrically re-released — and was a commercial success all over again.

events.title: Film and Television Institute of India Founded
events.blurb: A national school for cinema craft, established on the former premises of a shuttered studio whose golden era had passed, began training directors, cinematographers, and sound engineers in a new medium that independent India wanted to shape on its own terms. Its graduates would go on to redefine the aesthetic vocabulary of both art-house and popular Indian filmmaking.
events.revealBlurb: 1960, Pune. Built inside the Prabhat Film Company compound. Satyajit Ray advised on its curriculum. Early graduates include Shyam Benegal, Adoor Gopalakrishnan, Mrinal Sen, Girish Karnad — essentially the entire generation that invented Indian parallel cinema.

events.title: Hum Aapke Hain Koun..! Released
events.blurb: A fourteen-song, over-three-hour family wedding drama that critics pre-screened and privately predicted was an unreleasable disaster became, on release, the first Hindi film to gross ₹1 billion — selling 74 million tickets domestically, the highest footfall for any Hindi film since the 1990s. The industry pivoted overnight toward family-oriented, non-violent spectacle.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1994 — director Sooraj Barjatya, a sequel of sorts to his earlier Maine Pyar Kiya. Salman Khan and Madhuri Dixit were cast against type as wholesome leads. The film ran in a Mumbai multiplex for over three years without leaving screens.

events.title: KGF: Chapter 2 Released
events.blurb: A Kannada-language action sequel about a gold miner's violent rise and rule over an illegal mining empire released simultaneously in five languages, broke the opening-day records of every film before it in the Hindi belt, and became the first Kannada film to gross ₹1,000 crore — a moment that announced South Indian cinema's claim on the pan-India blockbuster market.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2022 — directed by Prashanth Neel. KGF Chapter 1 had been a slow-burn cult hit two years earlier; the sequel was designed from the outset as the louder, bigger answer. Yash, who plays Rocky, was a regional star of modest fame before Chapter 1; after Chapter 2 he turned down a reported 50 offers in a single week.
